'''''Syagrus romanzoffiana''''', the '''queen palm''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SYRO4|taxon=Syagrus romanzoffiana|accessdate=4 December 2015}}</ref> '''cocos palm''' or '''Jerivá''', is a [[Arecaceae|palm]] native to [[South America]], introduced throughout the world as a popular ornamental garden tree. ''S. romanzoffiana'' is a medium-sized palm, quickly reaching maturity at a height of up to {{convert|15|m|abbr=on|lk=in}} tall, with pinnate [[leaf|leaves]] having as many as 494 pinnae ([[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]]), although more typically around 300, each pinna being around {{convert|18|in|cm|-1|order=flip}} in length and {{convert|1|-|2|in|cm|0|order=flip}} in width.

== Etymology ==
Named after [[Nikolay Rumyantsev]] (1754–1826), who was [[Russia]]'s Foreign Minister and Imperial Chancellor and notable patron of the Russian voyages of exploration. He sponsored the [[first Russian circumnavigation]] of the globe.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

It was previously scientifically known as ''Cocos plumosa'', a name under which it became popular in the [[horticulture|horticultural trade]] in the early 20th century. In some areas of the world the plant is still [[common name|popularly known]] as the '''cocos palm'''.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

== Taxonomy ==
[[File:A cocos plumosos palm tree growing in a grassy lawn at the foot of the steps to a residence, Los Angeles, ca.1920 (CHS-1488).jpg|thumb|left|A 'Cocos plumosos' palm tree growing in a lawn in front of a residence in [[Los Angeles]], California in 1920.]]
This palm was first scientifically described and validly published as ''Cocos romanzoffiana'' in 1822 in Paris in a folio of illustrations made by the artist [[Louis Choris]], with a description by the French-German poet and botanist [[Adelbert von Chamisso]].<ref name=IPNI1>{{cite web |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=62631-2&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DCocos%2Bromanzoffiana%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2005 |website=International Plant Names Index |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, The Harvard University Herbaria, and the Australian National Herbarium |access-date=3 September 2018}}</ref> Both men had participated in the first [[first Russian circumnavigation|Russian scientific expedition around the world]] under command of [[Otto von Kotzebue]], and funded by [[Nikolay Rumyantsev]], during which they collected this plant in the hinterland of [[Santa Catarina (state)|Santa Catarina]], Brazil in late 1815.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

Meanwhile, in England, circa 1825, [[Loddiges]] nursery had imported seed of a palm from Brazil which they dubbed ''Cocos plumosa'' in their catalogue, a ''nomen nudum''. The horticulturist [[John Claudius Loudon]] in 1830 listed this plant among 3 species of the ''[[Coconut|Cocos]]'' [[genus]] then grown in Britain, and mentioned its possible identification as [[Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius|Karl von Martius']] [[Syagrus comosa|''C. comosa'']].<ref>{{cite book |last=Loudon |first=John Claudius |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/41105#page/406/mode/1up |title=Loudon's Hortus Britannicus. A catalogue of all the plants indigenous, cultivated in, or introduced to Britain |date=1830 |publisher=Longman, Rees, Orme, Brown, and Green |volume=copy 1 |location=London, England |page=381 |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.10320}}</ref> One of Loddiges' seedlings found its way to the new palm stove built at [[Kew Gardens#Palm House|Kew Gardens]] in the 1840s, where it had grown to a height of 50–60 ft, and where botanists determined it to be another of von Martius' species; [[Syagrus coronata|''C. coronata'']]. In 1859 this palm flowered and produced fruit for the first time, which made it clear that its previous identification was incorrect and thus the director of the garden, [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]], 'reluctantly' published a valid description for Loddiges' name ''C. plumosa'' in 1860.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hooker |first=Joseph Dalton |date=1 May 1860 |title=''Cocos plumosa'' – Feathery-flowered Cocoa-nut |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/14362#page/82/mode/1up |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |series=3 |volume=86 |issue=16 |at=tab. 5180 |access-date=3 September 2018}}</ref> ''C. plumosa'' became a popular ornamental plant around the world, and plants continued to be sold under this name as of 2000.<ref name="FNA">{{cite book |last=Zona |first=Scott |title=Flora of North America |date=2000 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-513729-3 |volume=22 |location=Oxford, England |page=121 |chapter=''Syagrus romanzoffiana'' in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200027120}}</ref>

From 1887 onwards [[Odoardo Beccari]] published a review of the genus ''Cocos''. Under subgenus ''Arecastrum'' he listed the taxa ''C. romanzoffiana'' of Santa Catarina, ''C. plumosa'' known only from cultivation from seedlings from the plant in Kew, ''C. australis'' of Argentina to Paraguay, ''C. datil'' of eastern Argentina and Uruguay, ''C. acrocomioides'' of [[Mato Grosso do Sul]], ''C. acaulis'' of [[Piauí]], [[Goiás]] and recently collected from the mountains of Paraguay bordering Brazil, and ''C. geriba'' (syn. ''C. martiana'') known as a variable species cultivated in gardens throughout Brazil ([[Rio Grande do Sul]], [[Minas Gerais]], [[Paraná (state)|Paraná]], [[Rio de Janeiro (state)|Rio de Janeiro]]) and the Mediterranean region. Beccari noted that many of the palms being offered in the catalogues under various species names were actually ''C. geriba''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Beccari |first=Odoardo |date=1888 |title=Le Palme incluse nel genera ''Cocos'' Linn. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/105499#page/92/mode/1up |journal= Malpighia -rassegna Mensuale di Botanica |language=it |volume=2 |pages=85–90 |access-date=8 September 2018}}</ref>

In 1912 [[Alwin Berger]] reduced the taxon ''C. plumosa'', hitherto still only known from thousands in cultivation around the world yet not known from the wild, to a variety of ''C. romanzoffiana'', as ''C. romanzoffiana'' var. ''plumosa''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Berger |first=Alwin |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/42312#page/121/mode/1up |title=Hortus Mortolensis : enumeratio plantarum in Horto Mortolensi cultarum |date=1912 |publisher=West, Newman |location=London, England |page=87 |trans-title=Alphabetical catalogue of plants growing in the garden of the late Sir Thomas Hanbury at La Mortola, Ventimiglia, Italy |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.10950}}</ref>

It was first moved from the genus ''Cocos'' in 1891 by [[Otto Kuntze]] in his [[Revisio Generum Plantarum]], which was widely ignored, but in 1916 Beccari raised ''Arecastrum'' to a monotypic genus and synonymised all species in the former subgenus to ''A. romanzoffianum''. By this time South American imports of palm seed were being sold across Europe under a plethora of names, according to Beccari often mislabelled but impossible to determine down to 'correct' geographical species, thus he interpreted the taxa to belong to a single extremely variable species. This interpretation was long followed. Beccari also considered ''C. botryophora'' part of this species, an interpretation that is now partially rejected. Beccari recognised the following, now rejected, varieties:<ref name=Beccari2>{{cite journal |last=Beccari |first=Odoardo |date=1916 |title=Il genere ''Cocos'' Linn. e le palme affini |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/181342#page/20/mode/1up |journal=Biblioteca Agraria Coloniale |volume=10 |language=it |pages=14–32 |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.101655 |access-date=9 September 2018|doi-access=free }}</ref> 
*''Arecastrum romanzoffianum'' var. ''australe'' – from ''C. australis'', ''C. datil''
*''Arecastrum romanzoffianum'' var. ''botryophora'' – from ''C. botryophora''. As this taxon Beccari (mis)identified plants growing in [[Rio de Janeiro]] he earlier considered ''C. geriba''. Synonymy later rejected. 
*''Arecastrum romanzoffianum'' var. ''ensifolium'' – from ''C. botryophora'' var. ''ensifolium'' of [[Bahia]].
*''Arecastrum romanzoffianum'' var. ''genuinum'' – nominate form. Includes ''C. romanzoffiana'', ''C. plumosa'', ''C. geriba'', ''C. martiana''.
*''Arecastrum romanzoffianum'' var. ''genuinum'' subvar. ''minus'' – from a dwarf individual plant of uncertain origins in cultivation in a private collection in [[Hyères]], France.
*''Arecastrum romanzoffianum'' var. ''micropindo'' – from a population of dwarf plants from Paraguay earlier misidentified as ''C. acaulis''.
Beccari also reinstated Martius' ''Syagrus''.<ref name=Beccari2/>

''Arecastrum'' was subsumed under ''[[Syagrus (plant)|Syagrus]]'' in 1968.

A [[genetics]] study by Bee F. Gunn found that ''S. romanzoffiana'' did not group with the other two ''Syagrus'' species tested, but with ''[[Lytocaryum weddellianum]]''.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Gunn |first= Bee F. | date= 2004 | title=Phylogeny of Cocoeae (Arecaceae)...etc. |journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden | volume=91 | issue=3 |pages= 505–522 | jstor= 3298627}}</ref> If this has merit, then ''L. weddelianum'', being the junior taxon, becomes ''Arecastrum weddelianum''.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

== Distribution ==
[[File:Palmeras en Trenque Lauquen (plantas 01) foto 06.JPG|thumb|left|upright=1.2|''Syagrus romanzoffiana'' can grow in tough urban conditions. This picture is of the city of [[Trenque Lauquen]], Argentina.]]
It occurs from eastern and central [[Paraguay]] and northern [[Argentina]] north to eastern and southern [[Brazil]] and northern [[Uruguay]].<ref name=r/><ref name=Brazil2020/><ref>Lorenzi, H., Noblick, L.R., Kahn, F. & Ferreira, E. (2010). Brazilian Flora Arecaceae (Palms): 1–268. Instituto Plantarum de Estudos da Flora LTDA, São Paulo, Brazil.</ref> It is also native to [[Bolivia]].<ref name=IUCN/> It is quite common in its native range.<ref name=Brazil2020/>

In Brazil it occurs in the states of Bahia, Distrito Federal, Goiás, Mato Grosso do Sul, Espírito Santo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina.<ref name=Brazil2020/> In Argentina it occurs in the provinces of Buenos Aires, Chaco, Corrientes, Entre Ríos, Formosa, Mendoza, [[Misiones]] (El Dorado, Guaraní, Iguazú), Santa Fe, San Juan and San Luis.<ref name=Conosur/> In Uruguay it occurs in the departments of Maldonado, Montevideo, Rivera, Rocha, Salto, Tacuarembó and Treinta y Tres.<ref name=Conosur/> In Paraguay it occurs in the departments of Alto Paraná, Amambay, Caaguazú, Canindeyú, Central, Concepción, Cordillera, Guairá, Ñeembucú, Paraguarí and San Pedro.<ref name=Conosur/><ref>{{cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=16 June 2011 |title=Tropicos – Name – ''Syagrus romanzoffiana'' (Cham.) Glassman |url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/2401308?projectid=44 |access-date=10 September 2018 |website=Inventario Biologico de Paraguay |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden}}</ref>

=== Non-native distribution ===
The queen palm is reportedly naturalized to some extent in [[Florida]],<ref name=FNA/> [[Queensland]], Australia,<ref name="Dowe">{{cite book |last=Dowe |first=John Leslie |url=http://www.univpgri-palembang.ac.id/perpus-fkip/Perpustakaan/Geography/Biogeography/%5BJohn_Leslie_Dowe%5D_Australian_Palms_Biogeography,%28BookFi.org%29.pdf |title=Australian Palms: Biogeography, Ecology and Systematics |date=2010 |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |isbn=9780643096158 |location=Collingwood, Victoria |page=253 |language=en}}</ref> [[Honduras]], and the island of [[Mauritius]].<ref name=TimeBombs>{{cite journal |last1=Meyer |first1=Jean-Yves |last2=Lavergne |first2=Christophe |last3=Hodel |first3=Donald R. |date=January 2008 |title=Time bombs in gardens: invasive ornamental palms in tropical islands, with emphasis on French Polynesia (Pacific Ocean) and the Mascarenes (Indian Ocean) |journal=Palms |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=71–83 |s2cid=82225824 |url=http://www.palmeraie-union.com/pdf/palms.pdf }}</ref>

On Mauritius seedlings have been recorded from gardens in the now highly residential area 'Montagne Ory' near the village of [[Moka]] from 1981–1984 to at least 1999.<ref name=TimeBombs/>

The government of the [[Australia]]n state of Queensland considers it a potential 'invasive plant', and discourages home-owners from planting it, but it is not prohibited or restricted, or a declared weed.<ref>[http://www.dpi.qld.gov.au/documents/Biosecurity_EnvironmentalPests/IPA-Cocos-Queen-Palm-PP73.pdf Cocos or Queen palm Fact Sheet], Queensland Government, Australia, February 2013.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.daf.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0019/52831/IPA-Cocos-Queen-Palm-PP73.pdf |title=IPA-Cocos-Queen-Palm-PP73 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2016 |website=Invasive plant and animal fact sheets |publisher=Biosecurity Queensland |access-date=5 September 2018}}</ref> According to the 1989 Flora of Southeastern Queensland, it is naturalised in southern Queensland and the [[Atherton Tableland]].<ref name=Dowe/>

It is not regarded as an invasive or naturalised in [[New South Wales]],<ref name=Dowe/><ref>{{cite web |last=Wilson |first=K. L. |date=January 2013 |title=NEW SOUTH WALES FLORA ONLINE |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&showsyn=&dist=&constat=&lvl=gn&name=Syagrus |access-date=6 September 2018 |website=PlantNET (The NSW Plant Information Network System) |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust |publication-place=Sydney, Australia}}</ref> although numerous sightings of it have been recorded around Sydney and the coast, including in nature parks.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/atlaspublicapp/UI_Modules/ATLAS_/atlasreport.aspx |title=OEH Atlas of NSW Wildlife |date=2018 |publisher=Office of Environment & Heritage |doi=10.15468/14jd9g |access-date=6 September 2018|type=Data Set }}</ref> It has been classified as a [[noxious weed]] by one local council in New South Wales since at least 2010;<ref>{{cite report |url=https://www.agrifutures.com.au/wp-content/uploads/publications/10-216.pdf |title=Evaluating Biodiesel Potential of Australian Native and Naturalised Plant Species |author=Ashwath |first=Nanjappa |date=December 2010 |publisher=Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation |pages=49–51 |docket=10/216 |access-date=7 September 2018}}</ref> as of 2015 it is not prohibited or restricted in the state, but classified as a 'serious threat ... not widely distributed in the area in one local region.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Thorp |first1=John R. |last2=Wilson |first2=M. W. |date=January 2015 |title=Weeds Australia – Weeds Database Search |url=http://weeds.ala.org.au/noxious.htm |access-date=6 September 2018 |website=Weeds Australia |publisher=Australian Weeds Committee, Invasive Plants and Animals Committee}}</ref> It was possibly first identified as a potential environmental weed for the area in a book from 1998.<ref name=TimeBombs/> Sale is discouraged and the palms are being removed.

It is widely planted throughout much of [[Florida]] and other parts of the southern [[United States]], although it is not yet widely established in the flora as of 2000.<ref name=FNA/>

It can also be found in some parts of the Mediterranean basin.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

== Ecology ==
[[File:Syagrus romanzoffiana Treinta y Tres, Quebrada de los Cuervos, Bosque de Quebrada 7.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|''Syagrus romanzoffiana'' growing in the wild in Bosque de Quebrada, Uruguay.]]

It is a common tree in many habitats.<ref name=Brazil2020/>

Birds are recorded to eat the fruit pulp from fallen fruit include the [[rufous-bellied thrush]] (''Turdus rufiventris''),<ref name=Guix1>{{cite journal |last1=Guix |first1=Juan Carlos |last2=Ruiz |first2=Xavier |date=1995 |title=Toucans and thrushes as potential dispersers of seed-predatory weevil larvae in southeastern Brazil |journal=Canadian Journal of Zoology |volume=73 |issue=4 |pages=745–748 |doi=10.1139/z95-087 }}</ref> the [[bananaquit]] (''Coereba flaveola''), [[violaceous euphonia]] (''Euphonia violacea''), [[Brazilian tanager]] (''Ramphocelus bresilius'') and [[tropical parula]] (''Parula pitiayumi''). [[Azure jay]]s (''Cyanocorax caeruleus'') feed on the fruit pulp both picked directly from the infructescence as well as from fallen fruit lying on the ground, usually swallowing the fruits whole or transporting them away from the tree.<ref name=dispersal>{{cite journal |last1=Silva |first1=Fernanda R. da |last2=Begnini |first2=Romualdo M. |last3=Lopes |first3=Benedito C. |last4=Castellani |first4=Tânia T. |title=Seed dispersal and predation in the palm ''Syagrus romanzoffiana'' on two islands with different faunal richness, southern Brazil |journal=Studies on Neotropical Fauna and Environment |date=1 December 2011 |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=163–171 |doi=10.1080/01650521.2011.617065 |s2cid=85989354 }}</ref> The two toucans ''[[Ramphastos vitellinus]]''<ref name=Guix1/><ref name=dispersal/> and ''[[Green-billed toucan|R. dicolorus]]''<ref name=Guix1/><ref name=dispersal/> pluck ripe fruits directly from the infructescence and regurgitate the seeds, the gamefowl chachalaca ''[[Ortalis guttata]]'' (or a closely related species, depending on one's taxonomic interpretation)<ref name=dispersal/> and the two related guan ''[[Penelope obscura]]''<ref name=Guix2>{{cite journal |last1=Guix |first1=Juan Carlos |last2=Ruiz |first2=Xavier |date=1997 |title=Weevil Larvae Dispersal by Guans in Southeastern Brazil |journal=Biotropica |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=522–525 |doi=10.1111/j.1744-7429.1997.tb00047.x |s2cid=85038659 }}</ref> and ''[[Penelope superciliaris|P. superciliaris]]'',<ref name=Guix2/> did so as well, but spread the seeds in their defecations and thus may be important dispersers.<ref name=dispersal/><ref name=Guix2/>

The squirrel [[Sciurus ingrami|''Guerlinguetus brasiliensis'' ssp. ''ingrami'']] is an important seed predator of this palm where the ranges of the two species overlap; breaking the nut open with its teeth at one of the three pores in the top of the nutshell. It preferentially targets bug-infested nuts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alves |first1=Briza Cristina |last2=Mendes |first2=Calebe Pereira |last3=Ribeiro |first3=Milton Cezar |title=Queen palm fruit selection and foraging techniques of squirrels in the Atlantic Forest |journal=Biotropica |date=March 2018 |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=274–281 |doi=10.1111/btp.12530 |s2cid=90076507 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Galetti |first1=Mauro |last2=Paschoal |first2=Maristela |last3=Pedroni |first3=Fernando |date=February 1992 |title=Predation on palm nuts (''Syagrus romanzoffiana'') by squirrels (''Sciurus ingrami'') in south-east Brazil |journal=Journal of Tropical Ecology |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=121–123 |doi=10.1017/S0266467400006210 |s2cid=84502876 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mendes |first1=Calebe Pereira |last2=Cãndido-Jr |first2=José Flávio |date=June 2014 |title=Behavior and foraging technique of the Ingram's squirrel ''Guerlinguetus ingrami'' (Sciuridae: Rodentia) in an Araucaria moist forest fragment |journal=Zoologia (Curitiba) |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages= 209–214|issn=1984-4670 |doi=10.1590/S1984-46702014000300001 |doi-access=free |hdl=11449/109719 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alvarenga |first1=Cibele A. |last2=Talamoni |first2=Sõnia A. |date=September 2005 |title=Nests of the Brazilian squirrel ''Sciurus ingrami'' Thomas (Rodentia, Sciuridae) |journal=Revista Brasileira de Zoologia |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages= 816–818|issn=0101-8175 |doi=10.1590/S0101-81752005000300048 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=de Vivo |first1=Mario |title=Mammals of South America Volume 2, Rodents |last2=Carmignotto |first2=Ana Paula |date=January 2015 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0226169576 |editor1-last=Patton |editor1-first=James L. |edition=1 |location=Chicago, Illinois |pages=13–15 |chapter=Family Sciuridae G. Fischer, 1817 |doi=10.7208/chicago/9780226169606.001.0001 |editor2-last=Pardiñas |editor2-first=Ulyses F.J. |editor3-last=D'Elía |editor3-first=Guillermo}}</ref> A long term study into feeding behaviour of this squirrel in a secondary [[Araucaria moist forests|''Araucaria'' forest]] found that although in certain seasons other plants were consumed in larger quantities, the palm nuts were eaten in large quantities throughout the entire year and were thus the most important food item.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bordignon |first1=Marcelo |last2=Monteiro-Filho |first2=Emygdio L.A. |title=Seasonal Food Resources of the Squirrel ''Sciurus ingrami'' in a Secondary Araucaria Forest in Southern Brazil |journal=Studies on Neotropical Fauna and Environment |date=1 December 1999 |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=137–140 |doi=10.1076/snfe.34.3.137.8910 }}</ref>

Other important seed predators are seed-boring weevils and [[Bean weevil|palm bruchid]] beetles<ref name=tapir>{{cite journal |last1=Olmos |first1=Fábio |last2=Pardini |first2=Renata |last3=Boulhosa |first3=Ricardo L. P. |last4=Bürgl |first4=Roberto |last5=Morsello |first5=Carla |date=1999 |title=Do Tapirs Steal Food from Palm Seed Predators or Give Them a Lift? |journal=Biotropica |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=375–379 |doi=10.1111/j.1744-7429.1999.tb00151.x |s2cid=86837066 }}</ref> of the genus ''Pachymerus''. Grubs of ''P. bactris'', ''P. cardo'' and ''P. nucleorum'' have all been found within the seed of this species (among many other species of related South American palms).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Clarence Dan |last2=Zona |first2=Scott |last3=Nilsson |first3=Jan A. |date=January 1995 |title=Bruchid Beetles and Palm Seeds: Recorded Relationships |url=http://www.palms.org/principes/1995/vol39n1p25-35.pdf |journal=Principes |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=25–35 |access-date=4 September 2018}}</ref> The large, colourful weevil ''Revena rubiginosa'' appears to be the main seed predator in numerous areas.<ref name=Guix1/><ref name=dispersal/><ref name=Guix2/> It is thought to probably be a specialist seed predator of this palm.<ref name=Misinterp>{{cite journal |last1=Brancalion |first1=Pedro H. S. |last2=Rodrigues |first2=Ricardo Ribeiro |last3=Novembre |first3=Ana D. L. C. |last4=Gómez |first4=José M. |date=January 2011 |title=Are We Misinterpreting Seed Predation in Palms? |journal=Biotropica |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=12–14 |doi=10.1111/j.1744-7429.2010.00726.x |jstor=41058536 |s2cid=83901349 }}</ref> It infests the developing seeds before the fruits are ripe, while they are still attached to the infructescence, the grubs exiting the seed to pupate underground around the palm when the fruit fall.<ref name=Guix1/><ref name=dispersal/><ref name=Misinterp/><ref name=Anchylorhynchus>{{cite journal |last1=da Silva |first1=Fernanda Ribeiro |last2=Begnini |first2=Romualdo M. |last3=Lopes |first3=Benedito C. |last4=Castellani |first4=Tãnia T. |date=February 2012 |title=Temporal Variation in Seed Predation by Insects in a Population of ''Syagrus romanzoffiana'' (Arecaceae) in Santa Catarina Island, SC, Brazil |journal=Neotropical Entomology |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=17–21 |doi=10.1007/s13744-011-0002-z |pmid=23950004 |s2cid=14799708 }}</ref> Other weevils found to be seed predators of this palm are ''[[Anchylorhynchus]] aegrotus'' and ''A. variabilis'',<ref name=Anchylorhynchus/> but these species are also flower visitors and likely important specialized pollinators.<ref name="De MedeirosVanin2020">{{cite journal|last1=De Medeiros|first1=Bruno A. S.|last2=Vanin|first2=Sergio A.|title=Systematic revision and morphological phylogenetic analysis of ''Anchylorhynchus'' Schoenherr, 1836 (Coleoptera, Curculionidae: Derelomini)|journal=Zootaxa|volume=4839|issue=1|year=2020|pages=1–98|issn=1175-5334|doi=10.11646/zootaxa.4839.1.1|pmid=33056794 |s2cid=222837392 |url=http://publication.plazi.org/id/FFB09C30B8694B58FFF8FFBBFFF6FF83 }}</ref>

The fruit are eaten by [[South American tapir|tapirs]], which might be important seed dispersers,<ref name=tapir/> and some wild [[canids]] such as the [[pampas fox]]<ref>BACKES, Paulo & IRGANG, Bruno, ''Mata Atlântica: as árvores e a paisagem'', Porto Alegre, Paisagem do Sul, 2004, p. 133.</ref> and the [[crab-eating fox]].<ref name=dispersal/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rocha |first1=Vlamir J. |last2=Reis |first2=Nelio R. dos |last3=Sekiama |first3=Margareth L. |title=Dieta e dispersão de sementes por ''Cerdocyon thous'' (Linnaeus) (Carnívora, Canidae), em um fragmento florestal no Paraná, Brasil |trans-title=Diet and seed dispersal by ''Cerdocyon thous'' (Linnaeus) in a forest fragment in Paraná (Carnivora, Canidae) |language=pt |journal=Revista Brasileira de Zoologia |date=December 2004 |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=871–876 |doi=10.1590/S0101-81752004000400022 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Three studies in Brazil, in four locations lacking other large frugivores such as squirrels, peccaries, deer and tapirs, found coati (''[[Nasua nasua]]'') to be important seed dispersers in such areas.<ref name=dispersal/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alves-Costa |first1=Cecília P. |last2=Eterovick |first2=Paula C. |date=July–August 2007 |title=Seed dispersal services by coatis (''Nasua nasua'', Procyonidae) and their redundancy with other frugivores in southeastern Brazil |journal=Acta Oecologica |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=77–92 |doi=10.1016/j.actao.2007.03.001 |bibcode=2007AcO....32...77A }}</ref><ref name=DietCoati>{{cite journal |last1=Ferreira |first1=Giovanne A. |last2=Nakano-Oliveira |first2=Eduardo |last3=Genaro |first3=Gelson |last4=Lacerda-Chaves |first4=Adma K. |date=March 2013 |title=Diet of the coati (''Nasua nasua'') Carnivora: Procyonidae in an area of woodland inserted in an urban environment in Brazil |url=http://ipecpesquisas.org.br/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/Ferreira_et_al_2013.pdf |journal=Revista Chilena de Historia Natural |volume=86 |pages=95–102 |doi=10.4067/S0716-078X2013000100008 |access-date=9 September 2018}}</ref> The coati climb into the palm to get at the fruit,<ref name=dispersal/> which in one urban study was found in 10% of all stool samples, although it constituted only 2.5% of the total faecal matter.<ref name=DietCoati/> Other important dispersing mammals were agoutis (''[[Dasyprocta azarae]]''), which sometimes cache seeds. [[Big-eared opossum|Black-eared opossum]] (''Didelphis aurita'') and a russet rice rat (''[[Euryoryzomys russatus]]'') were also found among the fallen fruits.<ref name=dispersal/>

The leaves of this palm are consumed by the caterpillars of the butterflies ''[[Blepolenis batea]]'' in Uruguay in 1974, [[Brassolis astyra|''Brassolis astyra'' ssp. ''astyra'']], [[Brassolis sophorae|''B. sophorae'']] and ''[[Catoblepia amphirhoe]]'' in [[Santa Catarina State|Santa Catarina]] in 1968, while [[Opsiphanes|''Opsiphanes invirae'']], the nominate form or possibly subspecies ''remoliatus'', was recorded feeding on this palm in both these regions. [[Opsiphanes quiteria|''O. quiteria'']] was also recorded feeding on the leaves in Argentina in 1969.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Penz |first1=Carla M. |last2=Aiello |first2=Annette |last3=Srygley |first3=Robert B. |date=1999 |title=Early stages of ''Caligo illioneus'' and ''C. idomeneus'' (Nymphalidae, Brassolinae) from Panama, with remarks on larval food plants for the subfamily |url=http://images.peabody.yale.edu/lepsoc/jls/1990s/1999/1999-53%284%29142-Penz.pdf |journal=Journal of the Lepidopterists' Society |volume=53 |issue=4 |pages=142–152 |access-date=15 October 2018 |s2cid=87385813 }}</ref>

Larvae of the giant day-flying moth ''[[Paysandisia archon]]'' are known to attack the piths of this palm species, along with many other species, at least in Europe, where neither the moth nor the palm are native. It can kill the palm. It prefers other genera of palm with more hairy trunks like ''[[Trachycarpus]]'', ''[[Trithrinax]]'' or ''[[Chamaerops]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nic.funet.fi/pub/sci/bio/life/plants/magnoliophyta/magnoliophytina/liliopsida/arecaceae/syagrus/ |title=''Syagrus'' |last=Savela |first=Markku |website=Lepidoptera and some other life forms |access-date=8 September 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2018 |title=Bestimmungshilfe des Lepiforums – ''Paysandisia Archon'' |url=http://www.lepiforum.de/lepiwiki.pl?Paysandisia_Archon |access-date=8 September 2018 |website=Lepiforum |language=de}}</ref>

The caterpillars of the Indonesian butterfly [[Cephrenes augiades|''Cephrenes augiades'' ssp. ''augiades'']] and the Australian [[Cephrenes trichopepla|''C. trichopepla'']] may also feed on the leaves of this palm.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nic.funet.fi/pub/sci/bio/life/plants/magnoliophyta/magnoliophytina/liliopsida/arecaceae/arecastrum/ |title=''Arecastrum'' |last=Savela |first=Markku |website=Lepidoptera and some other life forms |access-date=15 October 2018}}</ref>

The bases of the pruned fronds remain on the tree for several months and could serve as a habitat for insects or snails.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

== Cultivation and uses ==
The queen palm is planted in many tropical and subtropical areas.<ref name=FNA/><ref>{{cite journal |last=Proctor |first=G. R. |date=30 November 2005 |editor1-last=Acevedo-Rodríguez |editor1-first=Pedro |editor2-last=Strong |editor2-first=Mark T. |title=Family 19. ARECACEAE (PALMAE) Palm Family in Monocotyledons and Gymnosperms of Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands |url=https://botany.si.edu/pubs/CUSNH/vol52web.pdf |journal=Contributions from the United States National Herbarium |volume=52 |pages=152–153 |issn=0097-1618 |access-date=5 September 2018}}</ref> It is popular as an ornamental tree and much used in urban [[landscaping]]. It is hardy, to -5 °C ([[Hardiness zone|zone]] 9a), but the dead fronds must be pruned to keep the tree visually pleasing.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENH-767/ST609: Syagrus romanzoffiana: Queen Palm |url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ST609 |access-date=2024-03-11 |website=Ask IFAS – Powered by EDIS |language=en}}</ref> In some areas the fallen fruit are known for attracting unwelcome insects.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

The palm is often cut down in Brazil to use the [[leaves]] and [[inflorescences]] to provide animal (cattle) [[fodder]], especially in times of drought.<ref name="Arizona">{{cite web |date=2012 |title=Palms on the University of Arizona Campus – University of Arizona Campus Arboretum |url=https://arboretum.arizona.edu/palmsmain#Syagrus |access-date=4 September 2018 |publisher=The University of Arizona}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hear.org/Pier/wra/pacific/syagrus_romanzoffiana_htmlwra.htm |title=''Syagrus romanzoffiana'' risk assessment |last=Daehler |first=C. |date=3 November 2005 |publisher=Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER) |access-date=5 September 2018}}</ref> The leaves are similarly used in Argentina.<ref name=Mansfeld>{{cite web |url=http://mansfeld.ipk-gatersleben.de/apex/f?p=185:46:7814115845872::NO::module,mf_use,source,akzanz,rehm,akzname,taxid:mf,,botnam,0,,Syagrus%20romanzoffiana,11010 |title=Mansfeld's World Database of Agriculture and Horticultural Crops |last=Kruse |first=J. |date=April 2001 |publisher=IPK |access-date=5 September 2018}}</ref> Its fruits are edible and sometimes eaten;<ref name=Arizona/><ref name=Mansfeld/> consisting of a hard nut surrounded with a thin layer of fibrous flesh that is orange and sticky when ripe. The flavour is sweet and could be described as a mixture of plum and banana.{{citation needed|date=May 2026}}

According to Blombery & Rodd [1982] people eat the unexpanded leaves of apical buds in some regions. Fallen fruits are fed to pigs, and palm trunks are often used in construction, frequently hollowed out to make water pipes or aqueducts for irrigation.<ref name=Arizona/> In 1920s Argentina, it was cultivated as a crop. The young buds are consumed as vegetables, pickled or preserved in oil. The trunk of the palm provides [[sago]].<ref name=Mansfeld/>
